  <entry>
    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32273v1</id>
    <title>On the Algebraic Structure of Lewis Carroll's Logic -- Behind the Looking Glass: A Mathematical Perspective</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T07:32:30Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32273v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32273v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Charles Ludwidge Dodgeson, better known by his literary pen name `Lewis Carroll', has a number of well known and cherished literary works to his credit, for example "Alice in Wonderland" and "Through the Looking Glass". Apart from this he is known to have a strong professional interest in mathematics and logic with an inclination towards an educational and recreational perspective.
  In this work we consider the algebraic structure behind Lewis Carroll's approach to classical logic and his logical puzzles. Starting with the arithmetic of $0$ and $1$, we develop the connections between Boolean-valued functions, sets and predicates, which we refer to as the "entangled trinity". This provides a common setting in which Carroll's approach and Boole's perspective can be understood. Particular attention is given to what is meant by "the conclusion" of a logical problem. We suggest a precise interpretation of a complete conclusion in terms of largest lower bounds involving only the predicates to be retained, thereby sharpening Carroll's approach. The role of natural language in choosing a suitable universe and identifying these predicates is discussed through a variety of examples. Finally, we present computerised solution methods, including the use of Boolean satisfiability solvers for larger puzzles.</summary>
    <category term="math.HO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

  <entry>
    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31804v1</id>
    <title>Research profiles and the mathematical landscape: A grassroots proposal for mathematics with AI</title>
    <updated>2026-10-22T18:41:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31804v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31804v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Repeated mathematical work with AI leaves behind corrections, failed arguments, and sometimes useful ways of asking questions. I propose keeping these in a research profile that the mathematician develops and controls. The profile marks parts of the mathematical landscape according to the researcher's understanding and makes those markings available to later work with AI. This suggests experiments with individual profiles, shared readings of papers, and graduate education. It also raises mathematical questions about the landscape itself: its connections, distances, and changes under discovery. I describe two examples, searching for branches of mathematics with a common base and recovering useful questions from the history of Floer theory. The aim is to give mathematicians something to try and a part in deciding how mathematical AI develops.</summary>
    <category term="math.HO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31335v1</id>
    <title>What the submission does not show: Complexifying cognitive offloading in students' mathematical work with LLMs</title>
    <updated>2026-10-22T14:22:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31335v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31335v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A common concern is that using large language models (LLMs) lets students offload mathematical work that tasks are designed to elicit. Yet such claims often rest on outcomes (e.g., submitted solutions), rather than on evidence of students' work with LLMs. We followed 23 first-year linear algebra students as they solved three differently designed homework tasks with LLMs. Drawing on self-regulated learning and choice-affluent environments, we interpreted each of 429 prompts as a trace of a regulatory event and compared 59 chatlogs with the problem solutions the students submitted. Prompts formed five structures, casting the LLM mainly as a solver, explainer, or validator. The mix of structures shifted across the tasks, and ten of the 15 students who completed all three tasks changed their dominant structure. Most final submissions stayed close to LLM output, including those that followed exchanges in which students had explained, conjectured, and checked their own ideas. We conclude that an LLM-aided submission is not a trustworthy marker of students' offloading of the mathematical work, and that offloading needs to be examined in each regulatory space and part by part rather than as a whole.</summary>
    <category term="math.HO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29713v1</id>
    <title>Will AI kill us all---or just make mathematicians obsolete?</title>
    <updated>2026-10-21T13:26:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29713v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29713v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>AI's recent advances have fueled predictions of human intellectual obsolescence and fears for the future of mathematics. I argue that, impressive as these achievements are, they do not establish AI's capacity to invent new concepts and theories or sustain autonomous recursive self-improvement. Human intelligence also involves judgment, imagination, and embodied experience that standard measures fail to capture. Mathematics extends beyond proving theorems: its creative core lies in conceptual discovery and understanding. AI can strengthen this enterprise, but realizing its promise requires protecting attribution, open exchange, confidentiality, and mathematical training. I propose an academic AI consortium to provide powerful research tools with enforceable guarantees safeguarding unpublished ideas.</summary>
    <category term="math.HO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>
    <published>2026-10-21T13:26:45Z</published>

    <author>
      <name>Sergiu Klainerman</name>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27395v1</id>
    <title>Counting Who Counts: Black Women Mathematicians in the United States</title>
    <updated>2026-10-19T23:39:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27395v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27395v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>For Black women in the mathematical sciences, histories have frequently been fragmented or omitted from official records, an absence that itself constitutes a form of exclusion. This project addresses this critical gap by constructing a curated dataset of 147 Black women who have earned doctoral degrees in mathematics and related mathematical sciences in the United States. By integrating archival research, institutional records, digital databases, and community knowledge, we establish a reproducible methodology for identifying, verifying, and documenting Black women mathematicians.
  We situate this dataset within a broader history of efforts to document Black mathematicians and describe how prior archival and community based initiatives informed its development. We then demonstrate the utility of the dataset through exploratory analyses of doctoral production, institutional pathways, undergraduate preparation, mentorship networks, and research areas. This revealed patterns including large concentrations of doctoral production among a small number of institutions and advisors. Additionally, our analysis highlights the vital role of Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) in preparing Black women who have earned doctoral degrees in the mathematical sciences.
  By transforming historical documentation into structured research infrastructure, this work provides a foundation for future investigations of mathematical communities using historical as well as mathematical, statistical, and computational methods. More broadly, the framework developed here offers a model for constructing datasets that support the study of underrepresented communities within the mathematical sciences.</summary>
